2014-08-14 · public pressure. Choi Kyung-hwan became deputy prime minister for the economy and finance minister in July 2014 and pressed publicly for lower interest rates, launching a stimulus package and warning that the economy stood between a leap forward and a recession. He said in public that he had not mentioned the base rate and that the central bank should get the hint. The bank's independence is written into the Bank of Korea Act, but the same reporting noted a long record of governments pressing it to cooperate: the May 2013 cut under a previous governor was also widely read that way, and in October 2010 a vice finance minister attended a rate-setting meeting to deliver the government's view of the economy. On 15 September 2005 the US Treasury named Banco Delta Asia, a bank licensed and supervised in Macao, a primary money laundering concern under Section 311 of the USA PATRIOT Act, and FinCEN proposed a rule cutting it off from US correspondent accounts. Treasury said the bank had served North Korean government agencies and front companies for more than 20 years, handled the bulk of North Korea's precious metal sales, and helped agents make multi-million dollar cash deposits and withdrawals. Treasury said the bank tailored its services to North Korea with little oversight or control, and Under Secretary Stuart Levey said Macao needs significant improvement in its money laundering controls. These are the allegations of the US authorities; the bank denied wrongdoing, and the finding is an administrative one, not a criminal conviction. current_paragraph: The Bank of Uganda issues the Ugandan shilling, and the Auditor General audits its accounts under section 43 of the Bank of Uganda Act. One case is recorded. A confidential 2018 Auditor General report to parliament said bank managers, including governor Mutebile, acted without guidelines, regulations or policies and may have intentionally neglected aspects of the closure and sale of at least seven commercial banks between 1993 and 2017, including Crane Bank in 2016 and 2017. These are the findings of a report, not court verdicts. Sudhir Ruparelia, dfcu Bank and Nile River Acquisition Company are named in the case, the last two as having received money, favours or contracts from the central bank. Parliament then put the bank through a public inquiry over the same closures. The Auditor General, John Muwanga, presented his special audit to the Speaker of Parliament on 27 August 2018; it had been requested in November 2017 by the chairman of Parliament's Committee on Commissions, Statutory Authorities and State Enterprises, and the bank had tried to stop it. It questioned how the bank spent over 400 billion shillings closing Crane Bank, half of it not recovered. The committee, chaired by Abdu Katuntu, took evidence from the governor, Emmanuel Tumusiime-Mutebile, his deputy Louis Kasekende and other officials from late 2018 into 2019, and on 1 November 2018 Katuntu sent the governor and deputy governor away for arriving without the documents. Mutebile told the committee on 12 November that the seven banks were put under resolution largely because they were insolvent, said he had never delegated his powers to agree the sale of Global Trust Bank to DFCU Bank, and said liquidation reports had been kept from him by junior staff, which raised the question in public of whether he was in charge of his own institution. The committee's report, finalised in February 2019, recommended individual accountability for the officials implicated; demands in Parliament for action against them later stalled. The bank's banknote printing contract is with Oberthur Fiduciaire, signed on 26 July 2018. Northern Trust supplies compliance, performance and risk analysis and a dashboard for watching the outside firms that invest its money, which is analysis and advice rather than management of the money. Uganda scores 34 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, and on paper the bank is among the less independent, 0.467 of 1 on a 42-rule measure of independence written into law.

current_paragraph: The Central Bank of Samoa issues the Samoan currency, which as of December 2025 is kept within a crawling band of 2 per cent or less measured against the US and Australian dollars. Samoa scores 35 of 100 on exposure to outside influence, where 100 means fully exposed, more exposed than 65 per cent of the 194 places with a figure. Its weakest side is corruption and secrecy around the bank, mainly because the country's laws hide who owns money and because of money-laundering risk in its banks. One finding is on record: a performance audit of government debt servicing carried out by the Samoa Audit Office in 2014 compared the due dates of government debt repayments with the dates the Central Bank of Samoa actually made them and found instances where repayments had been delayed. The same audit recorded that there was no formalised arrangement between the Ministry of Finance and the central bank, and its recommendations went to the Ministry of Finance, including that the two bodies formalise their responsibilities; no wrongdoing by any person is alleged in it. In April 2026 the government pressed ahead with changes to the bank's own law that would widen the Finance Minister's role and move some of the bank's rules into regulations. In a letter to the Attorney-General's office the bank said the changes had come as a surprise and warned they could weaken its independence, increase political influence and create legal uncertainty. The International Monetary Fund wrote to Finance Minister Mulipola Anarosa Ale Molio'o on 9 April 2026 warning that the reforms could weaken the bank's autonomy, and Prime Minister Laaulialemalietoa Leuatea Polataivao Schmidt rejected the warnings as outside interference. The bank was created in 1984, and its law has been changed three times since 1970, each change giving it more independence. Note Printing Australia's customer list says it has produced and supplied polymer banknotes to the bank, and BDO Chartered Accountants audited the financial statements for the year ended 30 June 2025.

Central Banking reported on 30 July 2004 that President Maaouiya Ould Taya had sacked the chairman of the bank, the day after sacking his whole economic team, and that Zeine Ould Zeidane, formerly an adviser to the president, was installed in his place. The report names neither the sacked chairman nor any reason and gives no calendar date, saying only that it happened on the Monday. It rests on a single account relayed from IRIN, so it is reported rather than confirmed. One case is recorded, from 2020 and 2021, and it is still an investigation. In July 2020 police working under the Nouakchott-Ouest prosecutor arrested six people, one of them a bank employee, over foreign currency taken from the central bank; early reports put the amount at about 1 million US dollars and later reports at 2.4 million, plus 500,000 dollars in counterfeit notes. The National Reserve Bank of Tonga Act, Chapter 16.12 in its 2020 revised edition, sets out how the government may steer it. Section 50(1) lets the Minister, with Cabinet's consent, issue the bank written directives, and section 50(4) requires him to put any disagreement with the Board over a policy it has determined to Cabinet, which then determines the policy the bank adopts. The Governor is protected in office: under section 11(3) he may be removed by Cabinet, on the Minister's recommendation made at the Board's request, only for permanent incapacity, serious misconduct or failure to perform his duties. It scores 36 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, and 0.733 of 1 for the independence written into its law, where 1 means the bank holds the power and 0 the government. In 2012 Iraq's Board of Supreme Audit examined the bank's daily auctions of dollars to banks and found that most transactions rested on fraudulent paperwork; the country's top auditor told US officials that up to 800 million dollars a week was leaving Iraq illegally, as reported by the US Special Inspector General for Iraq Reconstruction. In October 2012 the cabinet removed governor Sinan al-Shabibi and named a successor while a parliamentary committee was examining possible manipulation of the dinar and charging that bank officials were abusing the dollar sales. A committee member said arrest warrants had been issued for 30 people, including al-Shabibi and his deputy Mudher Saleh, and the Supreme Judicial Council confirmed warrants without saying what the charges were. The integrity committee's chairman said the inquiry was not about money but about procedures, while a member of the finance committee called it a political decision and not professional; al-Shabibi's defence called the case politically motivated. No court outcome was ever found, so nothing was proven; he died on 8 January 2022, and the bank mourned him as a distinguished former governor. One career move is on record, and it stays inside the public sector: on 14 March 2023 the governor appointed Faisal Wisam al-Heims as deputy governor, from the post of Director-General of the Trade Bank of Iraq, which the report describes as a state-owned bank, and he had also chaired the Iraq Securities Commission, a regulator, so neither side of the move is private finance. It holds 175.6 tonnes of gold, and the Board of Supreme Audit audits its accounts. Who prints the dinar rests on an encyclopaedia entry rather than anything the bank publishes: it says the 2003 series, still the basis of circulating notes, was printed by De La Rue.

current_paragraph: The Bank of Russia issues the ruble, and is one of the 63 central banks that own the Bank for International Settlements, the central banks' own bank. It scores 38 of 100, where 100 means fully exposed to outside influence, its weakest side being corruption and secrecy around it. Government pressure was reported in 5 of 37 quarters between 2010 and 2018, every time to cut rates or loosen policy. In October 1994 President Boris Yeltsin fired chairman Viktor Gerashchenko over his part in the Black Tuesday ruble crash and named Tatyana Paramonova in his place; the State Duma rejected her by secret ballot, 107 to 127, opponents saying the constitution barred hiring or firing the bank's chief without the Duma's approval. On 19 October 2005 the Moscow prosecutor's office indicted Alexei Mishin, chief legal expert at the bank's Moscow directorate, and a deputy department head of the tax service, for taking a bribe of 1 million US dollars; at the Moscow City Court on 17 April 2007 prosecutors asked for 15 years for Mishin and 12 years for the tax official Oleg Alekseev, but the verdict is not known, so nothing is proven. After Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Western countries immobilised the bank's assets held in their jurisdictions, put at around 300 billion euros worldwide, and on 12 December 2025 the European Union agreed to freeze 210 billion euros of them indefinitely, replacing six-monthly renewals that Hungary or Slovakia could veto. It holds 2,283 tonnes of gold and has swap lines, standing arrangements to lend each other currency, with China and with Kazakhstan, the latter signed on 28 May 2026 for up to three years. Oleg Vyugin, a First Deputy Chairman of the bank, also held private finance posts at Troika Dialog, Morgan Stanley Bank, MDM Bank, Binbank and Safmar Financial Investments; the CV listing them gives no dates, so the order of the moves is not established, and no ethics finding is recorded. Its accounts are audited by B1 - Audit LLC and by the Accounts Chamber of the Russian Federation. Goznak, owned entirely by the federal government under the Ministry of Finance, prints Russian money, though the page describing it does not name the bank as its customer.

current_paragraph: The Central Bank of the Comoros issues the Comorian franc, and France stands behind it. A monetary cooperation agreement signed at Moroni and Paris on 23 November 1979 rests on an unlimited French guarantee of the currency the bank issues. It set the rate at 1 Comorian franc to 0.02 French francs; after a devaluation of 33 percent on 11 January 1994, the rate is now 1 euro to 491.968 Comorian francs. The bank must keep 65 percent of its foreign currency reserves on deposit with the French Treasury. Two governments also fill its board. Under statutes signed in Paris on 22 April 2008 it had at most eight members, half named by the French government and half by the government of the Union of the Comoros, with the Governor named by the President of the Union on the finance minister's proposal. Under statutes in force since March 2025, France names two of the six board members, two of the four members of the banking supervision committee and two of the four on the committee that sets monetary policy and manages reserves.
